entry.summary: Hello everyone, I’ve developed an open-source tool called Leax. https://github.com/hooop/leax Leax combines Valgrind, GDB-based tracing, and Mistral AI to: The memory analysis itself is deterministic (based on execution traces), while the AI is mainly used to explain the “story” of memory in your program in plain language. It works well on classic C programs using malloc/free. There are still limitations in some cases (multi-process programs, etc.), and the tool is actively being improved. If anyone wants to try it on their C projects, I’d really appreciate feedback and suggestions! Thanks!

entry.title: Most users don’t search for a tool — they scan the page first
entry.summary: While building AllInOneTools, I expected users to behave in a simple way: User lands → uses search → finds tool → completes task. But watching real usage showed something different. Most users don’t start with search. They start with scanning. They scroll a little… Not because search is bad. But because visual recognition is faster than thinking. When users arrive on a tools website, they usually come with a task like: • Compress an image But instead of typing the tool name immediately, many users try to spot it visually first. If they see something like: Image Tools They instinctively move toward it. This happens within seconds. If users scan first, the homepage structure becomes extremely important. Clear categories All help users locate their task quickly. Without this, users hesitate. And hesitation often means they leave. On AllInOneTools, I started showing tools directly inside categories instead of only showing category names. That small change helped users confirm instantly: “Yes, my tool is here.” Confidence increased. Clicks increased. When users visit your website, do they: • Use search first? Would love to hear how others observe user behavior.

entry.title: Beginning of My Journey
entry.summary: Hello world! My name is Henry Han, and my Korean name is Sehun Han. I lived in Nicaragua for 15 years and attended an American school, which made me fluent in English, Spanish, and Korean. I love to work out, eat, go for drives, walk in parks, and enjoy anything related to keyboards. I am a Computer Science graduate from Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in South Korea. I was not very motivated at the time and got distracted by a lot of things. I have always regretted not trying my best during university; that feeling haunted me like a ghost. Even when I was working in other roles, such as Global Sales for a pharmaceutical company, I wasn't happy. I knew I had taken the role not because I was passionate about medicine, but because it was an easy way to avoid being jobless. About a month ago, I left my job to dedicate my time to studying programming, computer science, and everything dev-related. I know it will be a rough market to get a job, especially with AI replacing many junior positions. However, I decided that I didn't want to run away anymore from the dreams of my younger self: to be a genius programmer, just like the hackers in Hollywood movies. My plan is to study full-time for the next 1 to 2 years to land a junior developer role. My interests are in Backend development, and I created this blog for "Today I Learned" (TIL) posts and occasional journaling. I am open to all networking and am looking forward to learning from the community. Hopefully, I can become highly skilled in this field and return the generosity. Looking forward to start this journey, and also making friends along the way! 😊 P.S.: I do not want to put too much time in styling my posts (initially), so please excuse the messy formatting! P.P.S: I am not a fan of AI generated articles, as they don't feel genuine to me. Most of my posts will be raw, unorganized piles of thoughts that I will try to make sense of, make them readable, and enjoyable.
